deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Riemann's 1847 student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation', published posthumously in the Werke (1876). Throughout, Π(s)=Γ(s+1).

The previous page defined a value of the generalized derivative of order μ via the Taylor expansion of z about the point k:
  ^k p_μ(x) = Σ_{n≥0} z^{(n)}(k) (x−k)^{n−μ} / Π(n−μ).
In this series the coefficient of h^μ/Πμ is the derivative of the coefficient of h^{μ−1}/Π(μ−1), so it is a value of ∂^μ z.

Step 1. Differentiate with respect to k, treating x as fixed.
- Term n contributes z^{(n+1)}(k)(x−k)^{n−μ}/Π(n−μ) − z^{(n)}(k)(x−k)^{n−μ−1}/Π(n−μ−1).
- The sum telescopes, and only the n=0 negative term survives:
  dp_μ/dk = −z(k)(x−k)^{−μ−1}/Π(−μ−1).

Step 2. Fix the constant of integration.
- If μ<0, then n−μ>0 for every n ≥ 0, so every term of the series vanishes at k=x. Hence p_μ|_{k=x}=0.
- Riemann states 'Nun verschwinden alle Glieder ... für k=x' without the explicit condition; μ<0 is supplied by me here and is stated later.
- Therefore p_μ(k) = ∫_x^k (dp_μ/dk') dk'. This is legitimate when the integrand is integrable, i.e. z is continuous on [k,x] and the exponent −μ−1>−1, so the singularity at t=x is integrable.

Step 3. Rename the variable to t and flip the limits:
  (†) ^x∂^μ z = (1/Π(−μ−1)) ∫_k^x (x−t)^{−μ−1} z(t) dt = (1/Γ(−μ)) ∫_k^x (x−t)^{−μ−1} z(t) dt,  for μ<0.
This is the Riemann–Liouville fractional integral of order α=−μ with lower terminal k.

Step 4. Other orders from the same expansion.
- The value belonging to the same expansion for order μ−n is (1/Π(−μ+n−1)) ∫_k^x (x−t)^{−μ+n−1} z dt.
- This is consistent: differentiating in x lowers the order by one.

Step 5. Independence of the base point (modulo the 'system').
- Changing k to k₁ changes the value by
  (1/Π(−μ−1)) ∫_{k₁}^k (x−t)^{−μ−1} z dt.
- Expand by the generalized binomial theorem, using Π(−μ−1)/(Π(n)Π(−μ−1−n)) = C(−μ−1,n):
  = Σ_{n≥0} x^{−μ−1−n}/Π(−μ−1−n) · ∫_{k₁}^k (−t)^n z(t)/Π(n) dt.
- The integrals are finite constants, independent of x.
- So the difference has the form Σ_{m≥1} K_m x^{−μ−m}/Π(−μ−m). That is exactly the form of the 'system of values' (formula (6) of the previous page).
- Hence all base points give values in the same system. Riemann restricts the notion of derivative to this system.

Step 6. Result, formula 1:
  ^x∂^ν z = (1/Π(−ν−1)) ∫_k^x (x−t)^{−ν−1} z(t) dt + Σ_{n≥1} K_n x^{−n−ν}/Π(−n−ν),
with arbitrary finite constants K_n. The arbitrary part is called φ_ν, Riemann's notorious 'complementary function'.

Step 7. Remark: every φ_ν is also a φ_{ν−n} for positive integer n. Reindexing gives x^{−m−ν}/Π(−m−ν) = x^{−(m−n)−(ν−n)}…; more simply, φ_ν's terms x^{−m−ν} are of the form x^{−(m+n)−(ν−n)}, and m+n≥1.

Purpose: to reduce the abstractly defined generalized derivative (defined via the formal series z(x+h)=Σ ∂^μ z · h^μ/Πμ over μ ≡ ν mod 1) to a concrete integral formula. Properties and values for specific functions are then derived from it on the next page.
errors: The termination step at k=x tacitly needs μ<0 (so all exponents n−μ>0). Riemann invokes '−μ−1>−1' only for continuity of the integral; μ<0 is stated explicitly a line later, so this is a matter of order, not an error.

Unjustified step: the binomial expansion of (x−t)^{−μ−1} in powers of t/x converges only for |t|<|x|, i.e. when the interval [k₁,k] lies inside |t|<|x|. Riemann justifies the step only by the finiteness of the integrals. In general (e.g. 0 between k₁ and x, or |k|>|x|) the series need not converge. The conclusion that changing k only adds a φ-type term then holds only formally or locally.
The integrability condition actually needed is integrability of (x−t)^{−μ−1} near t=x, i.e. −μ−1>−1. 'Continuity' of the integral is the stated criterion; it is fine but loosely phrased.

The complementary-function framework (arbitrary K_n with infinitely many terms, convergence unaddressed) is the well-known weak point later criticized by Cayley (1880). It is not a computational slip on this page, but the uniqueness and convergence issues are left open (cf. Riemann's own footnote 2 on the next page).

results.what: Telescoping k-derivative of the generalized Taylor series Σ z^{(n)}(k)(x−k)^{n−μ}/Γ(n−μ+1), giving −z(k)(x−k)^{−μ−1}/Γ(−μ)
results.modern_name: Derivation of Riemann–Liouville integral from generalized Taylor series

results.what: Fractional integral of order −μ: (1/Γ(−μ))∫_k^x (x−t)^{−μ−1} z(t) dt with arbitrary lower terminal k
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1847/1876), building on Liouville (1832) and Abel (1823)

results.what: Change of lower terminal adds a series Σ K_n x^{−ν−n}/Γ(1−ν−n); definition of the derivative up to this 'complementary function' φ_ν

deep.surprise_reason: This is the page of Riemann's well-known 1847 student essay (published in the Gesammelte Werke 1876) in which the Riemann–Liouville integral and the complementary function are introduced. It is exactly what he is famous for in fractional calculus.

checkable.sympy: k,x,mu=symbols('k x mu'); n=symbols('n',integer=True,nonnegative=True); f=Function('z'); term=lambda n: Derivative(f(k),k,n)*(x-k)**(n-mu)/gamma(n-mu+1); simplify(diff(term(0)+term(1)+term(2),k) - (-f(k)*(x-k)**(-mu-1)/gamma(-mu) + Derivative(f(k),k,3)*(x-k)**(2-mu)/gamma(3-mu)))
checkable.asserts: Telescoping: k-derivative of the partial sum leaves only −z(k)(x−k)^{−μ−1}/Π(−μ−1) plus a boundary term at the top index.
The Riemann–Liouville integral (formula † with k=0, α=−μ) maps t^b to Γ(b+1)/Γ(a+b+1) x^{a+b}.
Coefficient identity used in expanding (1/Π(−μ−1))(x−t)^{−μ−1} = Σ x^{−μ−1−n}/Π(−μ−1−n) · (−t)^n/Πn.
The terms of φ_ν differentiate into terms of φ_{ν+1}, so the 'system of values' is stable under d/dx.

transcription_corrections: Garbled sentence 'Man sieht leicht, dass [-man-] jeder verschiedene, man dem k verschiedene Werthe giebt' should read 'Man sieht leicht, dass, wenn man dem k verschiedene Werthe giebt, verschiedene Entwicklungen von z(x+h) daraus hervorgehen'.
In the line '... (x−t)^{−μ−1} z_t {+hervor+} durch Addition von', the dt is missing after z_t; 'hervor' is an interlinear insertion above 'durch Addition'.
The phrase read as 'von x unabhängige[?] Grössen' appears on the image as 'x konstante Grössen' (i.e. constants with respect to x); the meaning is the same.
In formula 1 the summation is written with n=1 on top and n=∞ at the bottom (Riemann's habitual order), i.e. Σ_{n=1}^{∞}.
The left margin '(†)' is Riemann's own mark '(†)' / '(+)' preceding the displayed integral.
